subject: body
title: Lungs and Breathing
about: Deeper than Heart, Lungs and Bones: what the lungs take from the air (oxygen) and what you breathe out (carbon dioxide), the nose that cleans and warms air, the windpipe, the millions of tiny air sacs, the diaphragm muscle that pulls air in, hiccups, yawns, candles, breath clouds on cold days, why the left lung is smaller, and why clean air matters. Inside-the-body anatomy is a bridge topic beyond NC Grade 1; the nearest codes are PE.1.HF.3.1 and PE.1.HF.3.2 (heart and lungs in fitness), 1.NPA.2.1 (activity) and Science LS.1.1.1 (living things need air). Read it together: the tablet reads every card aloud while he puts a hand on his belly and breathes.
tip: Have him lie on his back with a stuffed animal on his belly and watch it ride up and down as he breathes.

cards.q: What do your lungs take out of the air you breathe in?
cards.note: Oxygen is a gas in the air that every part of your body needs. Your blood carries it from the lungs.

cards.q: Which used-up gas do you breathe out to get rid of it?
cards.note: Say CAR-bon dye-OX-ide. Trees take it in and give back oxygen, so trees and people help each other.

cards.q: Why is it good to breathe in through your nose?
cards.note: Tiny hairs and sticky stuff inside your nose catch dust. The nose also warms the air before it reaches your lungs.

cards.q: You are running hard. Which lets in more air quickly, your nose or your mouth?
cards.note: The mouth is a bigger opening, so it helps when your body needs lots of air fast.

cards.q: Air goes down a tube from your throat to your lungs. What is the tube called?
cards.note: Feel the ridges on the front of your neck. Those are stiff rings that keep the windpipe open.

cards.q: Inside your lungs, air fills millions of tiny sacs like little...?
cards.note: Oxygen passes from the tiny sacs into your blood. They are called alveoli.

cards.q: A big flat muscle under your lungs pulls down to suck air in. What is it called?
cards.note: Say DY-uh-fram. When it pulls down your lungs get bigger and air rushes in; when it relaxes, air flows out.

cards.q: Hic! What is happening when you get the hiccups?
cards.note: The diaphragm gives a sudden jerk and your throat snaps shut: hic! Hiccups usually stop on their own.

cards.q: You run and your breathing speeds up. Who needs all that extra oxygen?
cards.note: Busy muscles burn energy and need more oxygen. Lungs and heart both speed up to deliver it.

cards.q: Sitting still, about how many breaths do you take in one minute?
cards.note: Kids breathe about 20 to 30 times a minute at rest, faster than grown-ups. Running can double it.

cards.q: Blowing out candles, blowing bubbles and whistling all use what?
cards.note: Your belly and chest muscles squeeze the lungs and push the air out in a stream.

cards.q: You open wide and yawn. What does a yawn pull in?
cards.note: Nobody knows for sure why we yawn. Being sleepy or bored, or seeing a friend yawn, can start one.

cards.q: Which air is best for your lungs?
cards.note: Smoke from cigarettes and fires harms lungs. Step away from smoke and let a grown-up know.

cards.q: Your left lung is a little smaller than your right lung. Why?
cards.note: The heart tips to the left, so the left lung has a dent to make space for it.

cards.q: On a cold day you can see your breath. What is that little cloud?
cards.note: Your breath is warm and wet. Cold air turns the wetness into tiny drops, like a small cloud.

cards.q: You fall asleep. What do your lungs do all night?
cards.note: Your brain keeps your lungs breathing slow and steady, so you never have to remember to breathe.
